title: Short Stuff: Haint Blue
summary: Josh and Chuck explain haint blue, the pale blue paint used on porch ceilings in the Southeast and Low Country (Charleston, Georgia and South Carolina coasts). They describe haints, restless spirits in Gullah Geechee culture, and the folk belief that the blue tricks spirits into thinking the sky or water blocks their path. They cover the boo hag (a sleep-paralysis-style spirit that counts compulsively, e.g., rice thrown on a floor) and the plat eye (a shapeshifting spirit tied to buried Confederate treasure, which can be warded off with whiskey). They tie the blue to indigo, the Low Country cash crop tied to slavery and to Georgia's legalization of slavery.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to haint blue
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, and Josh notes a friend from Charleston has a haint blue porch ceiling. They introduce haint blue as a pale blue paint common on porch ceilings in the Southeast.

segments.title: What haints are
segments.summary: A haint is described as a restless ghost that has not moved on, tied to the Low Country culture of descendants of enslaved people from west-central Africa. Haints are described as more meddlesome than typical ghosts.

segments.title: Hoodoo protection and the boo hag
segments.summary: Hoodoo, root work, and conjure use herbs and haint blue to protect against haints. The boo hag is described as a spirit that sits on sleepers' chests and steals skin; it can be distracted by counting thrown rice, a trait compared to Eastern and Central European vampires.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a short break and return.

segments.title: Plat eyes and Confederate treasure
segments.summary: The plat eye is described as a shapeshifter that is hard to defend against, with whiskey poured out as a possible deterrent. Plat eyes are said to be ghosts of people murdered and buried to guard Confederate treasure, so searching for that treasure risks attracting one.

segments.title: Indigo connection and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts connect the blue to indigo, a Low Country cash crop tied to slavery and Georgia's legalization of slavery. They explain the blue resembles sky and water to trick spirits, close with remarks on the tradition's spread into mainstream décor, and sign off.
topics: blue as sky and water to deter spirits
